chunks: One is that if he were an Imam with ascertained infallibility, there must be explicit statements by the Messenger of Allah (s) and Amirul Momineen, Imam Ali Ibne Abi Talib (a.s) about him,

because infallibility can only be determined through the statement of another infallible entity. However, the Kaisaniyya do not claim an explicit tradition with this regard. Instead, they rely on weak instances, which have led them to confusion, but are far from being explicit words.

One is that Amirul Momineen (a.s) granted him the standard on the battle of the Camel in Basra, and his saying, “You are truly my son,” while Hasan and Husain (a.s) were also his sons. These instances do not establish his Imamate in any way, and rather, indicate his excellence and high position.
ai.seo_question: Why is explicit textual designation necessary to prove the Imamate of a specific leader in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi critiques the Kaisaniyya sect by asserting that infallibility (ismah) necessitates explicit textual designation (nass), which they fail to provide. He dismisses their reliance on ambiguous indicators, such as receiving the standard at Basra or being called 'son,' as insufficient to establish exclusive Imamate given the presence of other sons like Hasan and Husain. This highlights the Shia emphasis on clear, unambiguous designation over weak or general evidence.
